PART ONE
Heart & Mind
CHAPTER 01
When Worry Keeps
Returning
A conversation ends, but you keep going over what you said. A
bill arrives, and your thoughts move from this month's payment
to everything that might happen next year. You check
something once, then feel the need to check it again.
Worry can attach itself to a real responsibility. You care about
someone, need to make a decision, or have good reason to think
ahead. The difficulty comes when thinking about it no longer
helps you decide what to do, yet you cannot seem to stop.
You may have prayed about the same concern many times.
When it returns, you wonder whether you meant your prayer or
whether your faith is weaker than you thought. Before drawing
that conclusion, listen to the words Scripture gives people in
distress.
When you wish you could get away
In Psalm 55, the writer describes a pounding heart, trembling,
and the wish to escape somewhere quiet. He is living with
threats and the betrayal of a close companion. His distress has a
history; the psalm does not ask him to leave it out of his prayer.

14
Later, he says that he cries out morning, noon, and night. The
prayer has to be spoken again as the day goes on.
You can bring a recurring worry to God more than once.
Yesterday's prayer does not make today's concern unwelcome.
You might begin by naming what keeps coming back: a child's
future, a difficult conversation, a result you cannot yet know.
You do not have to describe it calmly for God to hear it.
Psalm 94 offers another brief prayer to return to:
When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my
soul.
Psalm 94:19, Berean Standard Bible
The surrounding verses speak about injustice, danger, and God's
help. The writer finds comfort while troubling circumstances
remain part of his life. This verse gives words to a hope you can
pray toward, even on a day when comfort feels difficult to find.
What Jesus says about tomorrow
In Matthew 6:25–34, Jesus speaks about food, drink, and
clothing. These are ordinary needs with real consequences.
When He asks whether worry can add an hour to a person's life,
He draws attention to its limits.
You can spend a great deal of effort trying to make an uncertain
outcome feel settled. Even after you have considered every
possibility, the appointment is still ahead of you, or the reply has
not arrived. More thinking may bring you back to the same
unanswered question.
Jesus directs His listeners toward the Father's knowledge of
their needs and toward seeking God's kingdom. At the end of the
passage, He acknowledges that today has trouble of its own.
Following Him does not require pretending otherwise.
This leaves room for planning. You can make a budget, prepare
for an appointment, or ask someone for advice. The question is

15
whether there is a useful action available now. Once that action
has been taken, you may still have to live with uncertainty.
That can be hard, especially when someone you love is involved.
Returning your attention to today's responsibilities may feel like
neglecting tomorrow. You can care deeply about an outcome
and still reach the limit of what you can do about it today.
The prayer Jesus prayed in distress
Luke 22:39–46 takes us to the Mount of Olives before Jesus'
arrest. He kneels and asks the Father to take the cup from Him,
then entrusts Himself to the Father's will. Luke describes
anguish and an angel strengthening Him.
Jesus names His distress and His request as He commits Himself
to the Father's will. His path to the cross is unique; it gives us no
formula for predicting our own circumstances. We can
nevertheless learn from the honesty of His prayer.
You may be unsure what entrusting a concern to God looks like.
It can begin with a plain prayer: “This is what I want to happen.
This is what I am afraid of. Help me know what to do today.”
You may need to pray those words again later.
In John 14:27, Jesus speaks of giving His peace to His disciples
before the events that will trouble them. His words offer a basis
for trust as they face what is coming. They are not a deadline by
which a worried reader must feel peaceful.
Give one concern your attention
If it would help, choose one worry and put it into a sentence. Try
to be specific enough to see whether it asks something of you
today. “I need to arrange transport for Tuesday's appointment”
has a possible next step. “What if the appointment changes
everything?” may be a fear you cannot answer in advance.
For a concern with an available action, choose a manageable
one. Make the call, gather the information, or ask for help with

16
the task. For something you cannot settle, consider when you
will next have useful information. Until then, you can
acknowledge the uncertainty in prayer and give some attention
to what is in front of you.
You may find this difficult. The worry may interrupt you again.
There is no need to turn the exercise into another standard you
have failed to meet. It is a way of considering what needs your
action and what you need support to carry.
If anxiety is interfering with sleep, work, relationships, or daily
activities, speak with a health care provider or mental health
professional. Prayer can remain part of your life while you
receive professional care.
Pause and reflect
Which concern keeps returning, even after you have thought it
through?
Is there a useful action you can take, or are you waiting for
something you cannot know yet?
What would you like to say to God without first making it sound
more faithful?
If someone you care about keeps worrying
Give them room to explain the concern without making them
defend why it matters. Ask whether they would welcome help
with a task, company while they wait, or someone to listen.
Follow their answer rather than deciding for them what should
bring relief.
Avoid making calmness a measure of their trust in God. You can
offer to pray together if they would welcome that. If anxiety is
disrupting their everyday life, encourage professional support
and ask whether there is a practical way you could help them
seek it.

17
A prayer
Father, this concern keeps returning. You know what I hope for and
what I fear might happen. Help me recognize what I can do today
and where I need help. When I begin going over the same questions
again, give me patience with myself and help me turn toward You.
Please care for the people and circumstances I cannot control. In
Jesus' name, amen.
For further reading: Psalm 55; Psalm 94:16–23; Matthew 6:25–34; Isaiah 41:8–10;
John 14:25–31; Luke 22:39–46.
Read also:
• When You Feel Afraid (p. 18), if a particular fear needs closer attention.
• When You Feel Alone (p. 23), if you feel you are carrying your concerns without
company.
